concepts.name: Redoing from a blank page is practice testing
Testing a redo on edge cases
Comparing the complexity of first and redo attempts

questions.prompt: Which way of going through your redo list counts as practice testing?

choices.text: Reread your old solution slowly until every line feels familiar
Watch the video solution again, taking notes on each step
Solve it from a blank editor, then compare with your old solution
Copy your old solution out by hand, line by line, from the file

questions.explanation: Practice testing means retrieving the answer from memory rather than reviewing it. Solving from a blank editor does that, and comparing afterwards shows your gaps. Rereading and re-watching are review, and Dunlosky's review rated rereading low utility.

questions.prompt: In Dunlosky and colleagues' review of learning techniques, which two were rated high utility?

choices.text: Practice testing and distributed practice
Rereading and highlighting
Interleaved practice and summarisation
Self-explanation and the keyword mnemonic

questions.explanation: The review rated practice testing and distributed practice high utility because they helped learners of many ages across many kinds of material. Interleaved practice, elaborative interrogation and self-explanation were rated moderate. Rereading, highlighting and summarisation were rated low.

questions.prompt: Explain why rereading your old solution is a poor substitute for redoing the problem.

model_answer.summary: Rereading only makes the solution look familiar. Redoing from scratch makes you retrieve it, which is practice testing, one of the two techniques rated high utility, and it shows you exactly where you are stuck.
key_points: Rereading was rated a low-utility technique
Practice testing, retrieving from memory, was rated high utility
Retrieval shows gaps you can't see while rereading
Redo from a blank page, timed, and only then compare with the first attempt

questions.explanation: Dunlosky's summary says practice testing boosts learning and helps learners find gaps in their knowledge. In an interview you must produce a solution, not recognise one, so practise the thing you will be asked to do.

questions.prompt: Which redo schedule applies distributed practice?

choices.text: Redo all three problems the same evening, straight after the first attempt
Redo each problem a few days after the first attempt, and again about a week later
Redo them only the night before an interview
Redo one problem ten times in a row until it is fast

questions.explanation: Distributed practice spreads study sessions out over time instead of massing them together. Redoing a problem a few days later, and again later still, spreads the practice. Same-evening or night-before redos are massed practice, which gives worse long-term retention.

questions.prompt: Explain why you redo problems from your redo list days later rather than straight after the first attempt, and what timing each redo shows you.

model_answer.summary: Spreading practice over time (distributed practice) was rated high utility and gives better long-term retention than cramming. A redo days later tests whether you can still solve it, which is the question an interview asks.
key_points: Distributed practice spreads sessions over time rather than massing them
It was rated high utility in Dunlosky's review
Spaced practice gives better long-term retention than cramming the same total time
Timing a spaced redo against the first attempt shows what you have retained, not what you just saw

questions.explanation: The same review rated practice testing and distributed practice highest. A redo list that combines them, from a blank page and a few days later, uses both. A quick time straight after the first attempt mostly measures short-term memory.

choices.text: `[[1, 3]]`; nothing, since touching intervals are merged correctly
`[[1, 2]]`; the second interval is lost when it touches the first
It raises `IndexError`, because `out[-1]` is read before anything is appended
`[[1, 2], [2, 3]]`; ask if touching intervals overlap, and if so use `<=`

questions.explanation: `2 < 2` is false, so the strict comparison keeps touching intervals apart and the result is `[[1, 2], [2, 3]]`. The Tech Interview Handbook lists adjacent intervals like `[[1, 2], [2, 3]]` as a corner case and says to confirm whether touching endpoints count as overlap. There is no `IndexError`, because `out and ...` checks for an empty list first.

questions.prompt: Your array-problem redo passes the example input. Which extra inputs does the Tech Interview Handbook's array cheatsheet tell you to test?

choices.text: Only a very large random input, to check that it runs fast enough
Only an already sorted input and a reverse-sorted input of the same size
Empty input, one or two elements, and repeated or duplicate values
Only negative numbers and zeros, where most sign bugs hide

questions.explanation: The cheatsheet's corner cases for arrays are empty sequences, sequences of one or two elements, sequences of repeated elements, and duplicate values. A large random input tests speed, not correctness on the edges where most redo bugs are.

At `i = 0`, `x = 3`: `3` isn't in the empty dict, so `seen` becomes `{3: 0}`. At `i = 1`, `6 - 3 = 3` is in `seen`, so it returns `[seen[3], 1]`, which is `[0, 1]`. Checking before inserting is why the same element is never paired with itself. Duplicates are one of the handbook's corner cases.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of the `two_sum` function above, with a dict, for n numbers?

choices.text: O(n²), because it compares every pair
O(n log n), because the dict keeps keys sorted
O(1), because dict lookups are constant time
O(n) on average: one pass with average O(1) dict lookups

questions.explanation: The loop runs at most n times and each dict lookup and insert is O(1) on average, so the total is O(n) average time, with O(n) extra space for the dict. The handbook notes that interviews use the average case for hash tables. Python dicts keep insertion order, not sorted order.

questions.prompt: Your first attempt at Two Sum used two nested loops; your redo uses a dict in one pass. Compare the time and space complexity of each and explain the trade-off.

model_answer.summary: Nested loops check every pair: O(n²) time and O(1) extra space. The dict version makes one pass with average O(1) lookups: O(n) average time but O(n) extra space. It trades memory for time.
key_points: Nested loops compare all pairs, which is O(n²) time
Nested loops need only O(1) extra space
The dict version makes one pass with average O(1) lookups, so O(n) average time
The dict needs O(n) extra space, so it trades memory for speed
The O(1) lookup is the average case; hash tables can be slower in the worst case

questions.explanation: The handbook's approach techniques suggest trying a hash map first when you need faster lookups, and its hash table page gives O(1) average search and insert. In your log, record both complexities, not just the times, so the redo shows the better approach as well as the faster typing.
